item.title: Inside Critical PHP Vulnerabilities That Have 70% Of The Internet At Risk
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: A pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the open-source programming language that powers much of the modern web, has forced…
item.content:encoded:
A pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the open-source programming language that powers much of the modern web, has forced governments and companies across the globe into emergency action. 

The vulnerabilities, identified as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative and flagged separately by Google’s cybersecurity wing Wiz, could potentially give attackers a direct path to a server’s file system or database. 

For an internet ecosystem built largely on top of open-source components, this is a code-red scenario. The vulnerabilities were flagged by AI, and a fix was issued on Wednesday afternoon.

The response has been unusually broad. Finland has shut down state internet services, while the Netherlands’ cybersecurity agency has taken its website offline. France, too, has temporarily taken certain websites down. 

India’s CERT-In (Computer Emergency Response Team) and the US National Security Agency (NSA) have also advised organisations using PHP to update their systems or take their affected systems offline until immediate patching is not possible. Japanese Prime Minister (PM) Sanae Takaichi, in a post on X, urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities. This led to some users experiencing issues accessing the website on Thursday. 

The episode is significant not only because of the severity of the flaws but also because of how they were found. OpenAI said its GPT-5.6 Sol model identified one critical flaw, while Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. 

OpenAI described the episode as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory”, arguing that the development demonstrates both the defensive potential of AI and the growing risk that the same capabilities could help attackers develop exploits faster.

For organisations running PHP-based websites, applications and APIs, the immediate priority is to identify exposure, apply vendor patches and assess whether systems may already have been compromised. The wider tech industry is also rushing to coordinate and mitigate any problems emerging from the fracas. 

So how did the two flaws, which affect nearly every website on the internet, suddenly come to light? 

More Than Half Of Internet At Stake

PHP is a server-side programming language that is used to build websites and web apps. It processes user requests, connects to databases and often controls access to sensitive backend systems. Because it sits between the public internet and an organisation’s data, a flaw in PHP can have consequences far beyond a single website.

The newly disclosed vulnerabilities could allow attackers to reach a server’s file system or database. In practice, that means an attacker may be able to read, modify or delete files, access stored credentials, extract customer data or move deeper into an enterprise infrastructure.

At the heart of the crisis are two interconnected flaws rated 9.2 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity scale.

The bugs exploit deep memory-handling mechanisms inside the PHP execution core. This allows unauthenticated external attackers to send crafted web traffic, bypass security checks, and execute arbitrary code directly on the host server.

Making matters worse, these flaws aren’t restricted to modern builds. These vulnerabilities are believed to have existed in every version of PHP since version 5, which was first released in 2004. 

Websites running older versions face a more difficult upgrade path, as PHP 8.1 and earlier are no longer supported. The recommended fix is to move web servers to the latest version, PHP 8.5.12.

While the vulnerabilities were originally discovered by a joint team involving Google and OpenAI, the planned multi-month remediation timeline had to be rushed. After proof-of-concept details leaked prematurely on technical forums like Hacker News, PHP core maintainers were forced to rush out emergency builds ahead of the schedule.

“With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflexion point,” said Google Wiz in a post.

India Braces For Impact

India’s exposure is likely to be substantial because PHP remains widely used across government portals, educational institutions, small businesses, ecommerce platforms and legacy enterprise systems.

Many Indian organisations also rely on shared hosting providers, third-party web developers and older PHP-based content management systems. In these environments, the organisation using the website may not directly control the PHP version or patching cycle. As such, this could create a dependency on hosting providers and managed-service vendors to apply updates quickly.

The government’s own digital footprint could also be impacted. Many public-facing portals and state-run services often depend on PHP-based stacks. A vulnerability that potentially allows access to databases could also raise major concerns among the general populace.

The effect is already visible. As per website tracker DownDetector, websites like Airtel, Duolingo, Jio, Bank of Baroda, IRCTC, and State Bank of India, among others have been facing issues in the past few hours. 

As a result, CERT-In has issued an advisory for all “organisations and individuals using PHP. The agency has flagged “high risk of remote code execution and complete system compromise” due to these vulnerabilities. 

“These vulnerabilities exist in PHP due to memory corruption and improper resource control. A remote attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities by sending a specially crafted request to the targeted system. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code and compromise affected systems on the targeted system,” said CERT-In.

Going forward, Indian startups and companies will have the job of quickly identifying every PHP-based website and API in use. They will then have to apply the official patch as soon as it is available.

Where immediate patching is not possible, organisations should restrict public access, place affected systems behind a web application firewall, monitor logs for suspicious activity and consider temporary isolation. They should also review backups and recovery plans in case compromise is detected.

How Bad Is It?

The immediate operational impact could be disruption. Enterprises that cannot immediately patch vulnerable PHP systems could potentially have to take their systems offline until mitigation processes are complete.

For businesses, this can mean suspended websites, unavailable customer portals, delayed transactions and interrupted internal tools. For public-sector bodies, the risk extends to citizen services, government communications and critical administrative systems.

The government actions illustrate the scale of concern. As mentioned above, various bodies in Finland, the Netherlands and France have taken various websites down as a precautionary measure. 

The security consequences could be more damaging. If cyber attackers gain access to a server’s file system or database, they can potentially steal personal data, business records, authentication credentials or payment information. They could also modify website content, install persistent access tools or use compromised servers as a base for further attacks.

Cyberattacks In The AI Age

The PHP vulnerabilities show how quickly security has changed in the AI era. AI can now help researchers uncover flaws hidden in widely used software, giving defenders a chance to prepare fixes before attackers exploit them. 

At the same time, agentic AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploit development just as easily as it can support patching and threat detection. As models become more capable, the gap between a flaw being found and an attack being launched may shrink dramatically. 

This puts pressure on organisations to move from periodic security reviews to continuous monitoring, rapid patching and stronger default protections.

For organisations, the lesson is clear. Security can no longer be treated as an annual compliance exercise. Companies will need fast patching processes, least-privilege access controls, robust backups and incident-response plans. They must also assume that attackers may use AI to find and exploit weaknesses faster than before.

The PHP episode may be remembered less for the vulnerability itself than for what it signals. AI is becoming a central force in both offensive and defensive cybersecurity. The advantage will belong to organisations that use it to find, fix and prevent problems before adversaries can act.

item.content:encoded:
Serial entrepreneur Ajeet Singh, who previously cofounded unicorns such as Nutanix and ThoughtSpot, has announced the launch of his third venture, called Different. 

Emerging out of stealth mode, the AI-powered martech startup has now raised $48 Mn (nearly ₹453 Cr) in its seed funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from Lightspeed Venture Partners.

Meanwhile, former Asana executive Abhishek Pani and former chief technology and product officer (CTPO) at PharmEasy, Abhinav Yajurvedi, have also joined Singh as cofounders at Different. 

“Different is an AI marketing system that runs demand generation end-to-end for lean B2B marketing teams,” Singh said in a post on LinkedIn. The startup has teams in San Francisco and Bengaluru, per its website. 

Different aims to address enterprise bottlenecks such as hiring specialised talent, engaging multiple external agencies and managing disparate software tools. The startup’s AI platform plans, creates, executes and scales personalised content across channels in accordance with the business context, strategy, audience, and other parameters specified by the user. 

It also learns from the results and adjusts accordingly to optimise performance. Prior to its public launch, Different tested its services with early corporate customers, including software firms Descope and Motif. 

An alumnus of IIT Kanpur and IIM Calcutta, Singh has previously worked at companies like Oracle, Honeywell and PwC. Notably, this is not the first time that Singh is setting up his own business.

He previously also cofounded Nutanix in 2009, a hybrid cloud unicorn that went on to list on the Nasdaq in 2016. Singh stepped down from the company in 2012 to launch AI-powered analytics platform ThoughtSpot that same year. ThoughtSpot has raised over $670 Mn to date and was last pegged at nearly $4.5 Bn.

The development comes at a time when a growing number of founders are starting new ventures. Last month, Livspace founder Saurabh Jain and former executive Lalit Mittal banded together to launch a new venture, Gravity.

In May, Zeta founder Bhavin Turakhia launched a new AI startup, Neo, with a personal investment of $30 Mn. Prior to this, Healthians founder Deepak Sahni also said that he was building a new healthtech venture UN:BLOC.

Earlier this year in April, Inc42 reported exclusively that BharatPe cofounder Shashvat Nakrani was set to join Dubai-based luxury ecommerce platform Luxury For You as its cofounder and CEO.

item.title: eMudhra Weak Link Tests India’s Chain Of Digital Trust
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: A private key meant to vouch for the security of websites around the world turned out to be the number…
item.content:encoded:
A private key meant to vouch for the security of websites around the world turned out to be the number 4.

That was one of the weaknesses researchers found in eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates issued by Bengaluru-based eMudhra. 

The discovery prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft to block the affected certificates, triggering a wider effort to protect browsers, applications, and enterprise systems. The incident also rattled investors and eMudhra shares hit their 20% lower circuit at ₹431.55 on the BSE today. 

The immediate concern is whether software still trusting the compromised keys could accept fraudulent certificates. A related challenge is replacing legitimate certificates affected by browser makers’ decision to withdraw trust in a parent certificate.

A digital certificate acts as a digital identity that allows a browser to verify a website’s authenticity. Certificate authorities issue these certificates and vouch for their authenticity. eMudhra is among the certifying authorities licensed by India’s Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA). 

The incident goes beyond one company. It shows how much of the internet’s security rests on a chain of trust that one weak link can undermine, raising questions about how India oversees companies that participate in this global infrastructure.

What Happened

On October 17, a researcher named Wayne notified the Chrome Root Program, which forwarded the report to Mozilla, and also contacted eMudhra and the Apple and Microsoft root programmes, reporting that he had obtained the private keys corresponding to eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. He demonstrated control of each key by signing a message with it “We have a problem here – Wayne”.

The full details of how the flaw was discovered and fixed have now been published by Dennis Jackson, a cryptographic engineer at Mozilla.

Intermediate CAs can issue certificates that websites use to establish their identity. Anyone holding the corresponding private keys could potentially issue fraudulent certificates for websites they did not control, allowing affected clients that still trusted those CAs to accept the certificates.

The keys were not stolen, but the researcher found that they had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them easy to reconstruct from the public certificates.

Six of the eight intermediates were intended for website security through TLS, while two were intended for software signing. Chrome, Apple, Microsoft, and Firefox blocked the affected TLS intermediates.

What eMudhra Says

In a statement on its website, eMudhra said it was investigating the incident and reviewing its security controls and operating procedures. The company said the eight intermediate CAs were created during a key generation ceremony on April 30, 2025, and the hierarchy entered browser trust lists in mid-2025. It said its roots and issuing CAs had undergone independent audits in each of the previous two years, but did not identify the auditors or disclose the scope of those audits.

eMudhra said only one of the eight affected intermediates had been deployed in production and that none had issued end-entity certificates. It said it revoked all eight intermediates and was working with affected customers and root programmes to address the incident.

The company also said the incident did not affect its Indian Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) and eSign businesses, which operate on infrastructure separate from its global TLS business. On October 21, eMudhra said the affected global TLS business accounted for around 1% of its revenue.

India faced a similar trust-related incident in 2014, following the misissuance of certificates for Google domains by the National Informatics Centre. At the time, Google restricted the India CCA root certificate in Chrome to a limited set of domains, including gov.in and nic.in.

eMudhra has been a licensed certifying authority under India’s IT Act since 2008. The company has also worked with public- and private-sector organisations, including banks and government agencies.

The company provides digital identity, authentication and security solutions to businesses, financial institutions and governments. Its services include digital signature certificates (DSCs), electronic signatures and tools that help organisations secure digital transactions and manage identities.

In India, its DSCs are used for activities such as filing documents with government portals, including GST, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and income tax systems. Its eSign services also support paperless digital workflows.

Many critical government websites, including the Aadhaar issuer UIDAI as well as websites of the Indian postal services and the income tax filing portal, use eMudhra certificates or other technology developed by the company.

Why It Matters Beyond eMudhra

Browsers and operating systems rely on lists of trusted certificate authorities. A compromised intermediate CA can therefore threaten trust beyond the authority’s direct customers.

With the compromised keys, an attacker could potentially issue fraudulent website certificates to impersonate legitimate sites and intercept traffic, provided the affected systems still trusted those certificates and the attacker’s other technical requirements were met. The two code-signing intermediates also raised concerns about malicious software being presented as coming from a trusted publisher on systems that accepted their signatures.

“When news like this comes out about a company that supports our PKI infrastructure, it raises concerns about both the company’s reputation and the country’s reputation. Even a relatively small mistake or a gap in the validation process can affect confidence in the wider industry. People may start to question whether PKI infrastructure provided by Indian companies can be trusted,” said Abhijeet Zilpelwar, cofounder and chief technology officer at pi-labs.

The Long Tail: Software And Devices

Updated browsers received protections quickly. The harder problem is software and devices that do not receive the same updates or reliably check certificate revocation.

Applications, programming languages, package managers and build pipelines can use their own certificate bundles or the operating system’s trust store. Some do not reliably check revocation status, meaning they may continue to accept certificates unless their trust configuration or software is updated.

Embedded devices can be harder to update. Routers, cameras, payment terminals and industrial controllers running old firmware may continue to trust affected certificate chains if their software does not receive the relevant protections.

For Indian enterprises, exposure does not depend solely on whether they bought certificates directly from eMudhra. The company says none of the eight affected intermediates issued certificates to end users, and Google found no certificates chaining to the six website-security intermediates in public Certificate Transparency logs before blocking them. 

However, systems that continue to trust the affected intermediates may remain exposed if they lack effective revocation checks or have not received relevant security updates.

Potentially affected systems include backend applications, servers and devices running outdated software, including those operated by organisations that use another certificate provider. Banking, fintech, e-governance and other businesses relying on certificate-based authentication should assess their exposure, though the incident does not establish that these sectors have been disproportionately affected.

“Mid-sized organisations, SaaS providers and those with lots of vendor-managed systems are most exposed as they often do not keep track of their certificates,” said Rajesh Chhabra, general manager for India and South Asia at global cybersecurity giant Acronis.

The Ministry of Electronics and IT has issued a statement saying that the impact of this incident on Indian websites and applications have been very limited and for a very short interval. Additionally, the department has also formed a special team to investigate the matter and is engaging with relevant stakeholders.

According to CERT-In’s advisory issued on October 21, organisations should update browsers, operating systems and applications, ensure servers and devices receive current trust lists and revocation information, identify affected certificates and services, and replace them where necessary. CERT-In also advised organisations to verify certificate details and not bypass certificate warnings or disable certificate checks.

Venkata Satish Guttula, former director of security at Rediff.com India, said the eMudhra incident raised wider concerns about security audits. “Titles keep getting bigger while the people holding them get more junior. Audits look clean on paper, but the skill behind them is thin,” he posted on X, describing what he called an “illusion of competence” in security audits.

The post eMudhra Weak Link Tests India’s Chain Of Digital Trust appeared first on Inc42 Media.

item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: San Francisco-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith has raised $66 Mn in a Series C funding round led by Sequoia…
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith has raised $66 Mn in a Series C funding round led by Sequoia Capital, bringing its total funding raised till date to $125 Mn. Premji Invest and existing investors Peak XV Partners, Google Ventures, and Y Combinator also participated in the round. 

The startup raised the fresh capital at an unicorn valuation of $1 Bn, doubling in just over two months. It was valued at $550 Mn when Peak XV led its $45 Mn Series B funding round in August. 

In a statement, the startup shared plans to bolster its compute infrastructure and expand its technical engineering team. It says that it currently manages nearly 10 MW of compute footprint across data centers in the United States and Europe.

It shared plans to expand its total capacity by 5X in 2027 to meet growing enterprise demand.

“Even at the start of this year, we underestimated how much code people would be shipping. We expect that volume to only keep increasing as models get better and more engineers embrace AI codegen tools. We’re building Blacksmith to help developers merge code faster and feel confident about what they’re shipping,” Aditya Jayaprakash, Blacksmith’s cofounder and CEO, wrote in a post on LinkedIn.

Founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith operates a specialised cloud platform designed for automatically building and testing software code. It claims to serve more than 10,000 corporate customers worldwide, including high-growth tech firms such as Mercury, Granola, Supabase, and LangChain. 

As AI agents accelerate the speed at which code is written, the bottleneck for shipping software is moving from writing the code, to validating and testing code before deploying it – a step known as continuous integration (CI). 

Blacksmith claims its platform is tailor-made to absorb the spiky nature of CI demand with zero operational overhead, compared to general-purpose cloud infrastructure. 

According to the company’s blog post announcing the latest funding round, weekly CI jobs processed on Blacksmith jumped to over 90 Mn from 5 Mn back in January, driving a 17X jump in ARR over the same period.

item.content:encoded:
Update | October 21, 18:45 IST

Jio Platforms’ ₹30,213 Cr IPO closed its first day with 3.15X subscription, driven by strong demand from institutional investors. Investors bid for 62.3 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer.

The qualified institutional buyers’ (QIBs) portion was subscribed 9.42X, receiving bids for 46.15 Cr shares against an allocation of 4.9 Cr shares. Domestic financial institutions, including banks and insurance companies, accounted for the largest share of institutional bids at 25.92 Cr shares, followed by foreign institutional investors at 16.18 Cr shares.

The non-institutional investors’ (NIIs) portion was subscribed 1.68X, with bids for 6.11 Cr shares against 3.64 Cr shares reserved for the category.

Retail investors bid for 6.15 Cr shares against the 8.5 Cr shares on offer, translating to 72% subscription. It was the only investor category that was not fully subscribed on the first day.

The employee portion was subscribed 1.36X, attracting bids for 63.84 Lakh shares against 46.95 Lakh shares reserved. Meanwhile, the portion reserved for eligible shareholders of Reliance Industries was subscribed 1.45X, receiving bids for 3.24 Cr shares against an allocation of 2.23 Cr shares. 

Original | October 21, 2026, 09:15 IST

Reliance Industries’ digital services arm Jio Platforms saw its qualified institutional buyers’ (QIBs) portion fully subscribed within minutes of opening its IPO today, with the overall issue booked 58% in early bidding.

Investors placed bids for 11.48 Cr shares against 19.75 Cr shares on offer as of 09:45 IST, according to BSE subscription data.

The QIB category received bids for 9.57 Cr shares against 4.90 Cr shares reserved, translating into a subscription of 1.95X. Domestic financial institutions, banks, and insurance companies accounted for the bulk of institutional demand, bidding for 8.04 Cr shares, while foreign institutional investors bid for 1.28 Cr shares.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) bid for 45.43 Lakh shares against their allocation of 3.64 Cr shares, subscribing to 12% of the portion. Retail investors placed bids for 86.79 Lakh shares against 8.50 Cr shares reserved, booking 10% of their quota.

The employee portion was subscribed 26%, receiving bids for 12.30 Lakh shares against 46.95 Lakh shares reserved. Meanwhile, eligible Reliance Industries shareholders bid for 46.50 Lakh shares against their allocation of 2.23 Cr shares, translating to 21% subscription. 

The early institutional response follows Jio Platforms’ ₹8,109.8 Cr anchor round, in which it allotted about 7.25 Cr shares at ₹1,119 apiece. Participants included domestic mutual funds, insurers, and global investors such as BlackRock, the Government of Singapore, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.

Inside Jio’s Mega IPO

Jio Platforms has set a price band of ₹1,065–₹1,119 per share for the issue, which will close on Friday (October 23). At the upper end, it will raise ₹30,213 Cr (about $3.2 Bn), surpassing Hyundai Motor India’s ₹27,870 Cr offering to become India’s largest IPO. The pricing implies a valuation of around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr (about $108 Bn).

The offering comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr shares, with no offer-for-sale component. Jio plans to use ₹27,500 Cr to prepay certain borrowings of its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the balance earmarked for general corporate purposes.

The listing comes as Jio seeks to expand beyond telecom connectivity into fixed broadband, cloud services, enterprise solutions, and AI. Reliance Jio Infocomm had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, while its fixed broadband subscriber base stood at 28.6 Mn.

The company’s next phase of growth will depend on how effectively it converts this reach into higher earnings and paying customers for services beyond connectivity.

Jio Platforms’ operating revenue rose nearly 15% YoY to ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, while net profit grew 15.1% to ₹30,049 Cr.

item.title: eMudhra’s Security Key Flaw: What Went Wrong And Why Google, Mozilla Stepped In
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Eight private keys underpinning part of listed digital trust company eMudhra’s certificate infrastructure were so weak that researchers could recover…
item.content:encoded:
Eight private keys underpinning part of listed digital trust company eMudhra’s certificate infrastructure were so weak that researchers could recover them from publicly available certificates. The discovery prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft to block the affected certificates, triggering a wider effort to protect browsers, applications, and enterprise systems.

The incident also rattled investors. eMudhra shares hit their 20% lower circuit at ₹431.55 on the BSE today. 

The immediate concern is whether software still trusting the compromised keys could accept fraudulent certificates. A related challenge is replacing legitimate certificates affected by browser makers’ decision to withdraw trust in a parent certificate.

Here is what happened, how the flaw arose, and what it means for businesses.

What Happened In The eMudhra Security Incident?

Digital trust company eMudhra disclosed that eight of its digital certificate authorities had a serious security flaw after a researcher discovered that their private keys could be reconstructed from publicly available certificates.  

The keys were not stolen from eMudhra’s systems but instead generated using extremely small numbers that were easy to guess. The eight values were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The discovery prompted major technology companies, including Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft, to block or distrust the affected certificates. The incident has also raised concerns about the security of systems that rely on digital certificates to establish trust online.

What Is eMudhra And Its Significance In The Digital Ecosystem?

BSE-listed eMudhra provides digital identity, authentication and security solutions to businesses, financial institutions and governments. Its services include digital signature certificates (DSCs), electronic signatures and tools that help organisations secure digital transactions and manage identities.

In India, its DSCs are used for activities such as filing documents with government portals, including GST, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and income tax systems. Its eSign services also support paperless digital workflows.

The company operates internationally as well, providing digital certificates that help websites establish secure connections with users by acquiring digital certificates. 

eMudhra said the incident affected its global website-security business, not its Indian DSC and eSign operations. Its Indian services run on separate infrastructure and continue to operate normally, according to the company.

How Were Keys Weakened? 

The problem began during a key-generation ceremony on April 30, 2025. According to eMudhra, a flaw in the process created a second set of weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. Staff mistakenly used the weak keys when preparing the certificates, and the company is still investigating the exact error.

On October 17, 2026, a researcher identified as Wayne discovered that he could reconstruct the private keys from publicly available certificates. He demonstrated control over each key by signing a message with it and reported the findings to browser security teams.

Mozilla independently recovered the same keys on the day of the report, confirming the vulnerability. The eight affected keys included six used for website security and two intended for code signing.

What Has eMudhra Said About The Incident & Its Impact?

eMudhra said its core infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached, and its physical and digital security controls remained intact.

The company said the incident was confined to eight intermediate certificate authorities and did not affect its root CA private keys or other intermediate authorities. It also said none of the eight affected authorities had issued certificates to end users or websites, an assessment it said was supported by public records of issued certificates.

The affected global TLS business contributes around 1% of eMudhra’s revenue. However, the company acknowledged that the reputational impact could not yet be quantified.

eMudhra said it was working with customers who might be affected to provide replacement certificates and prevent disruptions to critical services. Its investigation into the root cause and security controls is ongoing.

Meanwhile, the IT ministry (MeitY) has said that the impact of the incident on Indian websites and apps was very limited and for a very short interval. Additionally, the department has also formed a special team to investigate the matter and is engaging with relevant stakeholders.

How Could Compromised Keys Affect The Internet’s Security Infrastructure?

Digital certificates help browsers establish whether a website is what it claims to be. They are a key part of the security system that allows users to connect to websites over HTTPS.

If someone obtains a certificate authority’s private key, they may be able to create fraudulent certificates that make an unauthorised website appear legitimate. In certain circumstances, this could enable an attacker to impersonate a website and intercept or modify communications.

There is no public evidence establishing that the compromised keys were used in a successful malicious attack

Google said no certificates issued through the six affected website-security authorities appeared in public Certificate Transparency logs before the company blocked them. Chrome requires such records for publicly trusted certificates, helping prevent fraudulent certificates from being accepted by the browser.

Other software, including applications and devices that do not enforce the same checks or use updated certificate lists, could face different risks. 

India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that the compromised code-signing keys could be used to make malicious software appear to have been signed by a trusted publisher, extending the potential risk to software whose authenticity is verified through digital signatures. It asked organisations to consider applications, servers and devices that rely on certificate trust stores.

How Have Technology Companies Responded?

Technology companies have moved to block the affected certificates and update their systems.

  • Mozilla: Blocked the certificates in Firefox within hours of receiving the report. It also released browser updates and is updating its wider certificate store to protect other applications.
  • Google: Blocked the affected keys in Chrome and took additional steps to remove the eMudhra’s root certificate authority from its Chrome Root Store. The removal is scheduled to reach supported Chrome devices on October 27, 2026.
     
  • Apple And Microsoft: Took steps to distrust the affected certificates through their respective security and certificate-trust programmes.
  • Cloudflare: Updated critical services, shared certificate stores and products including Cloudflare One and Cloudflare Tunnel. The company said its investigation had not identified active exploitation of the vulnerability on its own services.

These measures are intended to prevent systems from trusting certificates linked to the compromised keys. However, organisations using separate or outdated certificate stores may still need to update their software and infrastructure.

What Should Businesses & Developers Do To Mitigate The Risk?

Businesses should check whether their websites and applications rely on the affected certificates and follow the relevant software vendors’ advisories. Google has asked website operators using certificates linked to emSign ECC Root CA – G3, which is eMudhra’s root certificate authority, to obtain and install replacement Transport Layer Security certificates from another trusted certificate authority before Chrome removes the root from its trust store on October 27. 

Developers and IT teams should also update affected certificate stores, software dependencies and applications. Cloudflare has warned that applications using their own certificate stores may require separate remediation, including rebuilding or redeploying affected systems. 

Developers should not disable certificate verification to work around resulting errors, as this would remove the security protection the updates are intended to restore.

What Happens Next? 

The incident has prompted scrutiny of eMudhra’s wider certificate infrastructure. Google said it is reviewing whether the company’s remaining certificate authorities should continue to be trusted by Chrome. 

eMudhra is still investigating how its key-generation process produced weak keys and why they were used in the certificates. Another unresolved question is whether the keys were accessed or misused by anyone else before the affected certificates were revoked. 

The issue has also snowballed into a wider debate about the viability of digital trust infrastructures. The Internet Freedom Foundation today said it is preparing representations for the IT ministry, the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) and CERT-In regarding the vulnerability.

item.title: Enterprise AI Startup AuxoAI Nets $20.7M To Strengthen Its FDE Team
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: San Francisco-based enterprise AI startup AuxoAI has raised $20.7 Mn (over ₹195 Cr) in a Series A funding round led…
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco-based enterprise AI startup AuxoAI has raised $20.7 Mn (over ₹195 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by NTTVC, a Silicon Valley VC firm backed by Japanese telco NTT. 

Industry executives including Norwest Venture Partners’ George Still Jr, ServiceNow CPO and COO Amit Zavery, and Charlesbank Capital Partners’ MD Giacomo Santina also joined the startup’s cap table. 

AuxoAI plans to utilise the fresh capital to deepen ecosystem partnerships, expand its talent pool of forward deployed engineers (FDEs), and invest in its proprietary technology and AI-native delivery capabilities, including its Damia platform. 

“Our vision is to build a new kind of AI company – one that combines human expertise, enterprise context and engineering to stay with the problem from the first idea through measurable outcomes in production. This investment gives us the opportunity to scale that model globally,” cofounders Arvinder Pal Singh, Amaresh Tripathy and Kabir Singh said in a joint statement. 

Founded in 2023, AuxoAI offers an enterprise AI platform that pairs its AI strategists and engineers with enterprise client teams to build custom AI workflows. 

It helps enterprises accelerate AI deployment with Damia, a platform it describes as an “AI workbench for enterprise delivery”. It combines a pre-built skill catalogue with tools that capture institutional knowledge to build a context layer. 

AuxoAI says that it is an AI-native Google Gemini Enterprise Transformation partner and an AWS advanced-tier partner. The San Francisco-based startup operates engineering and operational hubs in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

Over the past three years, the startup claims that it has worked with over 40 clients across manufacturing, healthcare, consumer goods, and telecom sectors to turn AI into measurable business outcomes. 

Early adopters, such as marketing firm Athlonearth and restaurant group Fogo de Chao, have deployed AuxoAI’s infrastructure to automate manual tasks, make better informed decisions, and shorten strategy-to-launch timelines. 

As enterprises increasingly turn to AI adoption to boost productivity, FDEs are becoming increasingly critical for customising AI deployments to the company’s needs. According to staffing firm TeamLease Digital, demand for FDEs has jumped nearly 800% over the past year. 

Startups such as Bolna use FDEs to accelerate enterprise onboarding and shape product development. While better automation could eventually reduce deployment complexity, fragmented enterprise systems make FDEs increasingly important to AI adoption.
